characterList.description: An older gentleman with medium-length gray hair parted on the side. He is wearing a white button-down shirt and a wristwatch. He sits in a tan wingback chair throughout the video.
characterList.name: John Badham

content_metadata.description: Analysis of a video featuring insights from John Badham on the impact of technology on filmmaking.

qAndA.answer: He acknowledges it is sad but believes digital filmmaking is here to stay.
qAndA.question: What is John Badham's opinion on the demise of film in filmmaking?

qAndA.answer: He sees the rise of independent filmmaking as a positive outcome, leading to more challenging and diverse stories.
qAndA.question: What does John Badham believe is a positive result of the shift in filmmaking?

qAndA.answer: He uses it as an example of high-quality storytelling being produced for television.
qAndA.question: Why does John Badham mention the show "The Newsroom"?

qAndA.answer: He uses an anecdote about Frankenheimer to emphasize the importance of continual learning and tackling new creative challenges.
qAndA.question: Why does John Badham mention his friend, John Frankenheimer?

qAndA.answer: He believes the future is bright for independent filmmakers and suggests they embrace new platforms and diverse storytelling formats.
qAndA.question: What does John Badham suggest about the future of filmmaking?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Well, there are huge changes.
I mean, just immense sea changes, you know, the technology alone, where you have people
now pretty well convinced that very little will ever be done on film again.
And you are sad about it, and you know that film can do amazing things still, but there's
that huge technology change that is not going away.
And you also have fewer movies being made.
These big, immense, tentpole movies that are being made, and that all look like comic books
because they are comic books.
And at the same time, isn't it exciting that we see a lot of independent films being made
by all the people that used to make the big movies, but they still want to make movies.
And so they're making them independently for very little money.
People are deferring salaries and doing things.
The actors love to do that because it's probably more challenging material.
And that's why you get a lot of wonderful actors doing that for very little money because
they love doing it.
There's also the excitement of that when I started, there were three television networks.
And when somebody suggested that they were going to make a fourth television network,
that Fox, that was, that's funny, that lots of luck on that.
Why do we need a fourth television network?
Well, how many do we have now?
And cable networks.
And there's so much more work out there, so many more films, there are television films,
but look at the quality of them.
The quality of the breaking bads, the boardwalk empires justified the newsroom, things like
this, that are really, really good storytelling and good drama.
And that's exciting that these opportunities are out there.
So people have to make a mind shift and say, okay, it's not all about theaters.
And film, there is really good storytelling to be done in all of these other venues.
And the world is not collapsing on us because there are fewer movies in the theater.
We adjust to not only our television sets, but our iPods, our iPhones, our Android devices.
We're watching entertainment on so many different levels.
And all of these opportunities are there.
People doing, you know, making series just for, just for the, you know, the iPhone or
the Android.
And isn't that great?
They don't need the big studios.
My dear friend, John Frankenheimer, once observed that he never had met a director who
learned anything about directing by not directing.
And that you always need to learn something and you need to keep fresh with your storytelling.
And sometimes taking on challenges that might be a television show you've never seen before
or maybe didn't care for, but still, you know, how do you, how do you meet that challenge
and, and, and make things work?
So you stay fresh, you know, like going to the gym.
The storytelling abilities of being able to make a story as long as it will hold as the
right length is, is a wonderful kind of format.
And if you want to do something in 20 minutes or something like that, then you can do that
too.
I mean, I used to work on the night gallery series where we'd have stories that would be
30 minutes long or one minute long.
And some of the one minute were like little jokes, little visual jokes.
But it was always designed as a format where let's let the story have a say on how long
it is.
And that's what we get now in with all of our different platforms.
You know, we can do little short things for YouTube that are a couple of minutes that

And, and we can do much longer things.

Interview Subject: John Badham

Job: Director
What they're known for: Saturday Night Fever, Wargames, Short Circuit, Stakeout, etc.

Topic:
In the second of a three part interview, director John Badham (Saturday Night Fever, War Games) sits down with Microfilmmaker Magazine to discuss his new book, John Badham on Directing. In this interview, he emphasizes the technology of filmmaking.

To read the MFM review of John Badham's new book, go to: http://www.microfilmmaker.com/wordpress/2013/09/johnbadrev/

For more information on MicroFilmmaker Magazine, go to: http://www.microfilmmaker.com
